title: Character Blueprint: The Broken Chord
text:
The Slums of Manila: Born a Dalakitnon (Elf variant) to a destitute family in the Philippines, his early signs of extreme Charisma and magical potential weren’t a blessing—they were a survival ticket.

Sold to the Corp: His starving parents sold him at a young age to a Mitsuhama entertainment subsidiary. He was placed into grueling, military-discipline idol trainee dorms for over a decade, stripped of his cultural identity.

The Universal Face: The corporation invested fortunes in extensive, bio-sculpting cosmetic surgeries and permanent physical alteration spells to completely erase his Filipino features, reconstructing him into an optimized, “pan-Asian” aesthetic optimized for international marketability.
crumbs: 2  **Character Blueprint: The Broken Chord**

title: Character Blueprint: The Broken Chord
text:
2. The Corporate Weapon (The Death Messengers)

The Star-Powered Grim Reaper: He debuted as the “Face” and lead vocalist of TXM (a.k.a. The Death Messengers). Under the glitz, they were an elite corporate asset team trained in intense combat magic and synchronized coordination.

The Living Ritual: The band’s massive stadium concerts were actually massive, collective Geomantic Rituals. The synchronized choreography and the raw emotion of 80,000 screaming fans were used to channel immense astral power into the corporate grid to rewrite the free will of entire metroplexes.
crumbs: 2  **Character Blueprint: The Broken Chord**

title: Character Blueprint: The Broken Chord
text:
3. Resistance

The Variety Show Spark: During a massive, highly televised Matrix reality challenge, he was paired with Hana (“Luna”), the center star of Wuxing’s girl group, Yueying. Off-camera, stripping away their public masks, they connected over shared experiences.

The Sabotage: He discovered that his corporate handlers planned a massive mega-ritual that would target and completely consume Hana’s group to absorb their astral power. He sabotaged a major live performance, shattered the ritual matrix, and vanished into the shadows.

title: Character Blueprint: The Broken Chord
text:
The Playstyles

Weaponized Charisma & Fluid Identity: In negotiations, he treats the smoke-filled room like a stage. He effortlessly fluid-shifts his presentation—even changing genders to perfectly target a Mr. or Mrs. Johnson’s psychological profile, completely dominating negotiations and dictating terms.

The “Stage-Craft” Combat: When combat goes loud, his movement is pure, high-speed stage choreography. He keeps distance with uncanny, rehearsed grace, preferring to cast spells or bolster allies from afar.

The Mic Drop: He favors avoiding combat when possible, and uses the minimum force necessary when unavoidable.

Team: Bast (Bast), Mamba (Dreamwalker), Ninja (ArrogantNinja), Velvet (WarDoctor), Yankee Doodle (Inirlan)
Difficulty: Veteran
Summary: While being in Amsterdam for one reason or another, the team got hired by two Johnsons – first to find some kidnapped trucks, then to look for clues why it happened. They headed to the last known location, passed the traffic jams via a flying car and found a gas station nearby, where they got in contact with two teenage girls and learned that the crime community of Ghent might be involved. So they brought them to their soccer game and heard of a warehouse shared between three factions, with one of them rumoured to be the perpetrators. With that they went to the double warehouse, where they scouted it astrally and went for the host, only to get surprised by a databomb and finding the system going into alarm mode. Fearing for their traces, the team acted quickly and attacked the warehouse with open firepower. Despite a team of mercenaries that waited in a container for a shipment joining in, the criminals in the warehouse proved no match, and after breaking the resistance, the team interrogated or mindprobed some survivors to find out that it was a paid gig with insider knowledge. title: 20 Questions: Velvet
text:
Q1: Origins & Lineage

Nature has gifted us with our base set of genetics. We are born with a set of facial features, skin tone, height, build, metatype, and even aptitudes. Where does your character come from, what is their lineage, who were their parents, and what did they inherit from them?

Kim Jin-Young was born in the flooded slums of Manila, Philippines, as a Dalakitnon—a rare, nocturnal elven heritage known for sharp, preternatural grace and deep obsidian irises. In the starving shantytowns of Tondo, extreme natural charisma and an innate Awakened spark were not celebrated gifts; they were a commodity and a survival ticket.


Q2: Development & Creators

Nurture makes its mark on our attitude and response to the world. Assuming they could speak, what would each of your character’s parents say about them?

His parents would have little to say beyond the memory of desperation. Facing famine and crushing corporate debt, they sold five-year-old Jin-Young to a talent scout from a Mitsuhama Computer Technologies entertainment subsidiary. His childhood was spent inside hermetically sealed corporate idol trainee dormitories in Neo-Tokyo, where grueling twelve-hour dance drills, combat choreography, and mental conditioning systematically stripped away his Filipino identity in favor of corporate obedience.


Q3: Historical Influences & Trauma

Some historical events leave a mark and shape us in profound ways. Pick a few events from recent Shadowrun history and ask where the character was at the time, what do they remember, and what were they doing?

Jin-Young’s defining trauma was the systematic, clinical erasure of his physical identity at age ten. Over four months in a Mitsuhama surgical facility, intensive bio-sculpting, bone shaving, cartilage realignment, and permanent tissue alteration spells carved away his original features to construct an optimized, universally marketable “pan-Asian” aesthetic. The physical pain of resetting bone cartilage and the psychological horror of looking into a mirror and seeing a stranger became his lifelong baseline.


Q4: Entry into the Shadows

How did your character get into shadowrunning, and why did they take that path?

Jin-Young debuted as the center vocalist and Face of TXM (The Death Messengers), a massively popular boy group. Behind the stadium pyrotechnics, TXM was an elite Mitsuhama black-ops asset team. Their 80,000-fan stadium concerts were secretly engineered Geomantic Rituals designed to harvest collective astral mana to rewrite corporate loyalty across entire metroplexes. Upon discovering that MCT planned a lethal mega-ritual in Singapore to consume Wuxing’s idol group Yueying, Jin-Young sabotaged the performance, severed the ritual matrix, and fled into the Singapore drainage conduits, resurfacing in Seattle’s shadows to survive.


Q5: Living Spaces & Sanctuaries

What has your character done to their living space?

Velvet maintains a secure, low-profile safehouse in West Seattle leased through a shell identity. Unlike the hyper-sterile, camera-monitored dormitories of his corporate youth, his sanctuary is quiet and grounded in physical stillness: tatami flooring, cedarwood wall panels, a low-slung table with a cast-iron kettle for brewing un-taxed roasted Tieguanyin tea, and the scent of dry sandalwood incense. No trid screens or smart-home AI assistants are permitted.


Q6: Beliefs & Convictions

What does your character believe in, what are their convictions, and why do they hold them?

Velvet practices a syncretic Shinto-Musok tradition, honoring kami and ancestral spirit ribbons. Having been manufactured and bought as a disposable commodity, his deepest moral conviction is the creation of un-monetized sanctuaries—quiet spaces of genuine empathy, mutual respect, and protection for broken people who have been discarded or exploited by corporate machine logic.


Q7: Flaws & Friction

What flaws does your character have that sets others on edge? What do you dislike most about your character’s personality?

Years of algorithmic training and Charisma 10/12 social engineering mean Velvet’s default reaction to stress is weaponized charm, acoustic modulation, and micro-expression manipulation. Teammates sometimes find it difficult to tell when Velvet is being genuine versus when an algorithmic performance mask is active. Furthermore, physical transformations via Cosmetic Control R2 induce acute somatic migraines and chronic cartilage aches that Velvet conceals behind a placid smile.


Q8: Megacorporate Relations

Are there any of the Big Ten that your character hates, and why?


Mitsuhama Computer Technologies (MCT): Universal adversary. MCT created, sculpted, and owned him. Their Asset Recovery divisons continue to hunt for their missing high-spec IP.
Wuxing Incorporated: Complex and dangerous. Wuxing holds Hana under contract; while not actively attacking Velvet, their corporate machinations treat both runners as leverage in Pacific Rim trade negotiations.
Aztechnology & Renraku: Viewed with cold professional wariness as predatory blood-magic and Matrix panopticons.



Q9: Network of Contacts

What is the story with your character and their contacts?


Hana (“Luna”) [Seattle / Neo-Seoul]: Center star of Wuxing’s Yueying. The genuine bond formed during a televised variety show off-camera sparked Velvet’s rebellion; protecting her remains his emotional north star.
Brynne Taggart [Seattle Fixer]: The first major fixer to contract Velvet in Seattle, testing his corporate polish in the gritty Redmond underworld.
Ni Ni Xiaolu [Triad Johnson]: An Octagon Triad operative with whom Velvet established a respectful, mutually lucrative shadow partnership over tea in Tacoma.
Whiskey [Street Doc]: A reliable back-alley surgeon in Seattle who understands the biological taxation of bio-sculpting and provides pain management without logging corporate medical files.
Claudette Laurier & Vincent Grisome: Scholarly and occult resources in New Orleans and Seattle aiding his initiation into deeper esoteric mysteries.
Guild of Freelance Assets: A sovereign magical conclave providing coven ritual backing and initiation support in exchange for dedicated monthly service.



Q10: Distinguishing Features

What does your character look like, and how do they present themselves?

In his unmasked state, Jin-Young is a lean, 165 cm elf with porcelain-smooth skin, stark white hair, and deep obsidian irises that hint at his birth heritage. Through Cosmetic Control (Rating 2) and high-fashion tailoring (Ares SecureTech Skinshield), he shifts into two primary public personas: - Lee Ji-yoo (She/Her): Soft, elegant, razor-sharp corporate consultant and negotiator. - Tanaka Ryo (He/Him): Clean, authoritative, masculine executive liaison.


Q11: Combat Doctrine & Style

How does your character approach combat when negotiations fail?

Velvet treats combat as synchronized stage choreography and battlefield geometry. Maintaining distance with uncanny grace, he bolsters allies via Inspire Competence and Increase Attribute, dispels opposing magical structures, and uses Channeling or Increase Reflexes when direct engagement is inevitable, minimizing unnecessary collateral bloodshed.


Q12: Morality & Limits

What lines will your character never cross?

Velvet will never participate in the exploitation or trafficking of children, nor will he assist megacorps in spiritual harvest or geomantic mind-control rituals against metahuman populations.


Q13: Daily Routine & Solace

How does your character spend quiet downtime between runs?

Downtime is spent away from crowds and cameras: visiting small street stalls in West Seattle for un-synthesized pork-bone broth, brewing loose-leaf tea, maintaining coven shrine wards, and meditating to spirit ribbons while resetting facial cartilage in front of a mirror.


Q14: Financial Philosophy

How does your character view nuyen and wealth?

Nuyen is purely fuel for autonomy and security. Velvet maintains a strict Hooder practice (Rating 3), funneling ¥3,000 monthly into community aid and refugee relief, viewing un-shared wealth as corporate poison.


Q15: Spiritual Tradition & Magic

How does your character perceive and cast magic?

Under the Shinto-Musok tradition, magic is not mathematical code or high-fantasy fireballs; it is experienced as shifting emotional hues in auras, whispering ancestral presence, and folded talismanic paper ribbons. Drain manifests as physical exhaustion, dry vocal cords, and somatic bone aches.


Q16: Relationship with Technology

How does your character interact with the Matrix?

Velvet treats the Matrix with cautious respect. He relies on an Erika Elite commlink with Comhack Securelink and P-ICE Nope! for encrypted communications, but leaves deep node intrusions and cybercombat to specialized deckers and technomancers.


Q17: The Ultimate Ambition

What is your character’s long-term goal in the shadows?

To amass enough magical prowess, political leverage, and underground syndicate alliances to permanently sever Mitsuhama’s reclaim claims, liberate Hana from Wuxing’s golden cage, and establish a permanent sovereign sanctuary for Awakened refugees.


Q18: Secret Vulnerabilities

What is your character’s greatest hidden weakness?

Velvet suffers from chronic somatic pain and tissue fatigue from continuous Cosmetic Control transformations and early bio-sculpting trauma. Furthermore, any direct threat to Hana can cause him to abandon calculated risk assessments in favor of desperate rescue maneuvers.


Q19: Identity & Gender Fluidity

How does your character navigate their shifting gender presentation?

Having been engineered to embody any market demographic’s ideal fantasy, Velvet views gender presentation as both an art form and an operational tool. Whether operating as Lee Ji-yoo (she/her), Tanaka Ryo (he/him), or un-sculpted Jin-Young (he/they), each persona is inhabited with complete psychological authenticity and respect.


Q20: The Shadow Legacy

When your character eventually leaves the shadows, how do they wish to be remembered?

Not as an idol, a corporate weapon, or a commodity on a balance sheet—but as someone who found their own voice in the dark and used it to protect others from being silenced.

title: Transaction
text:
The neon housing above the Redmond quick-mart shivered against the corrugated sheet metal every time the sulfur wind came off the Barrens, a rhythmic metallic rattle in the damp cold. Inside, heat radiated off the rusted coils of an automated soykaf brewer behind the scratched laminate counter, competing with the sour green glow of a pirated local grid terminal looping reruns of old Neo-Tokyo urban combat trids. Lee Ji-yoo set three certified credsticks on the counter beside a small paper sack of synthetic strawberry drops. The clerk’s dented cyber-optic stayed locked on his overhead feed, gears grinding in the socket as his blind thumb swept the sticks into the cash drawer, cheap corporate chrome clicking against the tin tray.
“Need a bag?” the clerk asked, his voice rasping through an artificial vocal box scarred by industrial soot.
“No,” she said. The voice was Lee Ji-yoo’s, soft, clear, and quiet, though the resetting cartilage in her throat still radiated a dull, grinding ache from the shift thirty minutes prior. She kept the oversized collar of the heavy oilskin coat pulled high, burying a jawline smoothed of any native human imperfection. The clerk’s cyber-optic whirred, its autofocus hunting for a clean lock across the shadowed bridge of her nose, caught by the strange, motionless poise beneath the grease-stained canvas. She slid the paper sack into her pocket, took a single wrapped hard candy, and stepped out onto the wet gravel beneath the rattling eave.
The wrapper tore with a brittle pop. She slipped the pink sugar sphere past her teeth, and the chemical strawberry flavor hit her tongue with a sharp, synthetic coldness that left an oily film over her enamel.
Jin-Young had been five years old when that specific coldness first touched his palate, arriving on the same rain-drenched morning as the talent suit from Mitsuhama. The man had stepped out of an armored black sedan into the grey Manila humidity, wearing a three-piece suit of dust-repelling charcoal weave that shed the mud of the Tondo floodway without a stain. He had walked through the narrow alley where the sewer ditches overflowed with brackish tide water, his polished calfskin boots stepping deliberately across the cinder blocks to avoid the spots where raw drainage pooled against the wooden shanties.
Inside the shack, the torrential monsoon rain drummed against the rusted tin roof with the steady force of thrown gravel. Jin-Young’s father sat on the edge of the wood-frame cot with his hands wedged tight between his knees, staring down at knuckles scarred from thirty years of shipyard welding along the Pasig canal. His mother stood by the single kerosene burner, where a dented aluminum pot of thin rice gruel simmered with bitter melon greens, her fingers twisting the frayed hem of her faded cotton shirt until the seams pulled taut against her knuckles.
The suit stood in the center of the dirt-floor room, completely dry, bringing with him the smell of sterile corporate air conditioning and expensive fabric protectant. His sensor specs threw thin green diagnostic reticles across Jin-Young’s face, measuring the distance between the boy’s temples and the precise curvature of his nasal cartilage. His gaze ignored the water pooling in the corner and the damp laundry hanging from the ceiling rafters, focusing entirely on the biological geometry before him.
“The expression is clean,” the suit said, his voice carrying the flat, measured detachment of a customs inspector checking freight manifests. His fingers were entirely dry as they hooked beneath Jin-Young’s chin, tilting the boy’s head toward the grey daylight leaking through the open doorway to verify the alignment of the cheekbones and the solid obsidian depth of the Dalakitnon iris against the light. “The subterranean variance has settled properly in the bone structure. The baseline deviation fits the primary export profile. We will claim the biological deduction under Section Twelve.”
“He’s quiet,” his mother whispered, her eyes locked onto the floor near the clay water jar where Jin-Young sat watching the silver thread on the suit’s cuffs. “He doesn’t cry. Even when the fever came last winter, he stayed quiet.”
The suit tapped the edge of a silver datapad with a manicured fingernail, checking the genetic telemetry feeds. “Compliance is factored into the initial grading matrix. The vocal geometry shows early resonance markers. The shaping spells will take cleanly to the cartilage before the pubertal growth cycle begins.” He spoke of cellular elasticity and corporate patent registrations with the same dry cadence vendors at the corner palengke used when weighing scrap iron on a hanging scale.
The man reached into his breast pocket and laid a heavy silver credstick on the rough wooden table.
“Ten thousand nuyen,” the suit said, the silver plastic gleaming bright and sterile against the stained grain of the wood. “Certified by Mitsuhama Financial Services. The remainder of the stipend will be held in corporate trust, payable upon completion of the secondary reconstruction cycle in Kyoto.”
The shack was completely silent except for the roar of the rain on the tin roof and the steady drip of water falling into an empty tin can behind the cot. Jin-Young’s father kept his eyes locked on his calloused hands, motionless on the rough mattress. His mother’s hand hovered above the table for two long seconds, her fingers trembling against the humid air before they closed around the cold silver casing, tucking it deep into her apron pocket.
“Gather his things,” the suit said.
“He has no things,” his father said, his voice dropping into the dirt floor between his feet.
The neighborhood children stood along the mud alley in the pouring rain, watching in silence as the suit led Jin-Young toward the waiting sedan. The car’s windows were dark smoked glass with the triple-rhombus crest of Mitsuhama etched into the corner. The driver opened the rear door, releasing a blast of refrigerated, dust-filtered air that made Jin-Young shiver through his thin cotton shirt.
The door sealed with a heavy pneumatic thud, cutting off the sound of the rain and the smell of the slum in an instant. Through the dark glass, Jin-Young watched his mother standing in the doorway of the shack, her right hand pressed flat over her apron where the credstick sat against her ribs. Her arms hung rigid at her sides. Her gaze remained fixed on the sedan’s rear tires as they churned through the grey sludge of the alley, throwing muddy spray against the corrugated tin walls.
The suit sat in the leather seat opposite him, opening a briefcase lined with velvet compartments. He reached into a small sealed cylinder and took out a pink sugar drop, holding it out between gloved fingers.
“For the ride,” the suit said, his voice smooth and neutral. “Keep it on your tongue. It prevents nausea during transit.”
The candy tasted of synthetic strawberry and cold industrial solvent, slick on the palate like wet plastic. By the time the sedan cleared the corporate security gates at the Manila airfield, the sweet chemical coating had numbed the roof of the boy’s mouth, leaving behind only the sterile taste of air conditioning and clean leather.
Ji-yoo stood beneath the shivering metal eave in Redmond twenty years later, the same synthetic strawberry film coating the back of her teeth. She spat the pink drop into the black sludge at the edge of the asphalt. It lay there, a small sphere of artificial color against the grime, before the sulfur rain began to wash its pink dye into the puddle.
She pulled the heavy canvas collar tight against the damp wind coming off the Barrens, adjusted the strap of her bag, and stepped out into the dark.

title: Faceless Mirror
text:
The cauterizer in Whiskey’s Touristville basement clinic had a worn heating coil that emitted a high, thin whine every time her boot tapped the foot pedal. The sound competed with the heavy iron intake fan in the street-level window, which rattled against its security mesh whenever an automated freight hauler passed on the avenue above. Tanaka Ryo sat on the edge of the stainless steel examination table with his coarse linen shirt bunched in his lap, teeth set against the dry heat as Whiskey pressed the glowing copper tip against a flechette graze across his left shoulder blade. The wound had come from a territorial skirmish with Halloweeners near the Redmond border two nights earlier, a close call in the dark that had left his leather riding jacket shredded. He took the burn without local anesthetic, saving every certified nuyen to route through encrypted proxy accounts to Hana in Neo-Seoul.
“Hold your breath,” Whiskey muttered, her forehead beaded with sweat beneath the harsh glare of the overhead surgical lamp. She kept her eyes locked strictly on the three-inch line of torn muscle, working with the rapid, unblinking economy of a field medic under fire. She had not glanced at his face once since he climbed onto the table, her breath hissing through clenched teeth as the copper iron sizzled against living collagen, sealing the wound in dense, charred layers while Ryo sat unmoving beneath the light.
The singed heat against his shoulder skin brought back the antiseptic chill of the Mitsuhama post-op ward in Tokyo fifteen years before.
In the Tokyo facility, his entire head had been wrapped in damp smart-gauze that pulsed with automated saline flushes every twenty seconds. He was ten years old, lying on a narrow recovery cot in the dark, listening through the acoustic partition as the lead biometrics team reviewed his morning telemetry with the flat detachment of mechanics testing tolerances on an engine block. They spoke of cheekbone elevation, lash curvature, and the precise angle of the upper lip in fractions of a millimeter. A bound hermetic spirit drifted in the astral space near the ceiling, its presence casting an icy draft across the boy’s exposed shoulders as it anchored the shaping spells directly into his growing facial cartilage. Jin-Young stared into the woven black fibers of the bandages, his facial muscles twitching against fresh dissolvable sutures as the nerve pathways were chemically re-mapped to trigger a stranger’s smile.
For three weeks after the initial bone shaving, the smart-gauze remained sealed over his face, soaking in binding washes that carried the sharp scent of acetic acid and synthetic collagen. When the chief surgeon finally stepped into the ward to discharge him, her diagnostic specs projected thin emerald grids across his chest and throat. She signaled the orderlies with a flick of her stylus.
“Sutures dissolved,” she said, her voice flat against the hum of the air scrubbers. “The secondary cartilage binding took without tissue rejection. Remove the dressing.”
The assistants peeled the wraps with brisk, practiced motions, each layer coming away with the dry rasp of peeling parchment as the cool hospital air struck raw, newly formed skin with an icy burn. When the final layer dropped away, his skin pulled tight across cheekbones broad, heavy, and foreign.
“Check the baseline alignment,” the surgeon instructed. An assistant held up a rectangular mirror of polished, brushed steel before the cot.
Jin-Young looked into the metal.
The child who had played in the Manila monsoon was gone, replaced by a smooth, mathematically balanced face that belonged to no native bloodline. On the diagnostic monitor behind the cot, two digital profiles glowed side by side: the delicate, narrow jawline of Lee Ji-yoo and the broader, commanding symmetry of Tanaka Ryo. Both personas shared the same shaved foundation, a neutral biological canvas designed to pivot in either direction under the focus of cosmetic spells. Jin-Young raised a trembling hand, his fingertips touching skin smooth as polished stone, and tried to form the wide, gap-toothed grin his mother used to laugh at in the Tondo shanty. His facial muscles refused to cooperate. The nerves had been rerouted through corporate templates; when he forced the expression, his lips parted into a stiff, perfectly measured curve, the rehearsed idol smile now stamped into his living tissue.
“Baseline within designated parameters,” the surgeon noted, tapping her pad. “Archive the original facial scans. Prepare the asset for vocal modulation training.”
“Done,” Whiskey said in the Touristville clinic, her voice rough as she lifted the copper tip from his shoulder and dropped the cauterizer onto the metal tray with a sharp, echoing clatter. “Clean seal. Don’t stretch the deltoid for forty-eight hours, or you’ll rip the scab.”
She peeled the yellow latex gloves from her hands with two sharp snaps, throwing them into the biohazard bin beneath the counter, and unbuttoned her blood-speckled canvas smock. The moment the smock caught on the wall peg, the clinical rhythm of the room died, leaving only the hiss of the intake fan and the sudden, heavy silence between them.
She stepped over to the deep industrial sink, turned the cold brass tap, and thrust her bare forearms into the running water. When she lifted her hands, her fingers were visibly shaking. She clamped both palms hard against the stainless steel rim of the basin, locking her elbows and throwing her entire body weight onto the metal until her knuckles turned bloodless white against the steel. She stayed there, leaning over the drain with cold water splashing across her wrists, her breath coming in shallow, ragged hitches.
Behind her, Ryo pulled his coarse linen shirt over his head, the fabric catching slightly on the fresh scab as he walked to the grease-spotted mirror above the counter. The reflection staring back from the cracked glass was Tanaka Ryo: dark hair brushed back, jawline level, eyes clear and steady under the buzzing fluorescent tube. He leaned closer to the glass, looking where the outer rim of his pupils thinned in the downlight, revealing the faint, persistent ring of deep obsidian—the un-sculpted birth baseline waiting beneath the masks. He reached into his pocket and set two certified credsticks on the instrument tray beside the cooling iron.
Whiskey did not look at the money. She kept her knuckles welded to the sink rim, staring down into the dark opening of the drain pipe as the cold water splashed over her wrists.
“You’re wearing the man today,” she said, her voice tight and strained against the heavy quiet in the basement. “It’s different. It’s too heavy in here.”
Ryo paused with his hand resting near the iron door latch. “Would it make it easier if I came in as Ji-yoo?”
“No,” she murmured, a low, raspy breath filtering through her teeth as she looked away from his reflection in the glass. “That might be worse. One of these days, you’re going to burn yourself down to the wire, and there won’t be enough skin left to sew back together.”
Ryo pushed open the heavy iron fire door and stepped out into the Touristville alley, letting the cold Seattle drizzle wash over smooth, unbroken skin without finding a single native crease to follow.

title: Dark Wings
text:
Under the hundred-thousand-watt daylight arrays of the Wuxing soundstage in Neo-Tokyo, the arena floor of Astral Athletics: Idol Showdown stretched across three acres of polished chrome obstacles, magnetized climbing lattices, and synchronized broadcast cameras. High in the acoustic rafters, fifty automated camera drones hovered like oversized beetles, tracking every metahuman leap and spell-assisted pivot for millions of viewers across the Pan-Asian Pacific feed. Tanaka Ryo stood at the western staging gantry in his unit’s charcoal and silver racing silks, his pulse held at a steady sixty beats per minute while the floor transducers pumped synthetic adrenaline anthems through the reinforced decking.
The secondary transformer bank beneath the sub-floor let out a high-pitched acoustic scream, its cooling lines rupturing under the load of the high-voltage lighting grid. The main breaker tripped with an explosive crack, killing the daylight arrays in an instant and plunging the three-acre soundstage into sudden, suffocating darkness. In the confusion of shouting stage managers and rebooting security feeds, Ryo slipped through a heavy acoustic fire door into the backstage corridors, guided by the low-light filters in his retinas. He navigated the labyrinth of soundproofed access tunnels, reached the private VIP green room at the end of the hall, turned the brass latch, and pulled the heavy door shut behind him.
Luna sat in the low armchair in the far corner of the unlit room, her white silk stage silks catching the faint amber glow of an emergency exit sign above the private washroom. In the astral space near the acoustic ceiling panels, the bound watcher spirit tethered to Ryo’s aura drifted in a slow, circular patrol—an icy draft that tracked his skin temperature, his blood pressure, and the cadence of his respiration, ready to ping corporate security at the first sign of physiological distress.
“You’re late,” Luna said, her voice stripped of the airy, manufactured brightness sold on the weekly broadcast feeds. A faint mechanical tick came from the cervical actuators in her neck as she turned her head toward him, her optical shutters clicking twice to adjust to the dim emergency lighting.
“The secondary corridor had security patrols scanning badges,” Ryo said. The syllables slipped out in the soft, breathy cadence of Lee Ji-yoo before he caught himself, forcing his larynx down into Tanaka Ryo’s rigid baritone. He sat on the arm of the leather couch opposite her, hands resting flat on his knees. In the absolute dark, away from the staging lights and corporate lenses, the tension in his throat held between his assigned profiles, the cartilage settling into an aching, neutral middle.
Luna raised a slender hand, her fingertips tracing the edge of her collarbone where Wuxing dermal plating met living skin, thin chrome seams splitting the porcelain surface in the red emergency glow. Across her collarbone, the corporate asset serial numbers were etched in fine silver leaf. “They adjusted the biometrics this morning,” she said, her voice flat and even against the hum of the ventilation. “Lung capacity up twelve percent for the aerial choreography. My chest cavity feels hollow, like an empty tin can.”
“They plane the cartilage first,” he said, the softer elegance of Ji-yoo’s phrasing still bleeding into the lower register. “Then the binding wash sets the tissue. It stays dry behind the ribs for the first year until the nerve endings stop firing.”
“Does it ever stop?” she asked, her eyes catching the faint red strobe from the ceiling smoke detector.
“No,” he said, the voice settling entirely into the raw, un-sculpted baseline. “You learn to stop checking the mirror.”
Luna leaned forward, her shuttering optics fixing on his throat in the gloom. She reached across the small space, her fingertips touching the back of his hand. Her skin was warm from the staging lights, but the fingers were rigid with micro-hydraulic joints that lacked the irregular, organic tremors of native metahuman flesh. Through the physical contact, the hollow in her aura pressed against his astral senses, most of her native essence cleared out to seat reflex boosters, internal telemetry lines, and sensory processing chips.
“You have both,” she whispered, her voice barely carrying above the low hum of the corridor air scrubbers. “Don’t you?”
The watcher spirit drifted closer in the astral plane, testing for any emotional spike or unauthorized vocal deviation, but Ryo kept his respiration perfectly level, his posture locked in place as the heavy transformer beneath the sub-floor began to whine back to life. Emergency beacons along the wall baseboards flickered from amber to green.
“Hana,” she whispered into the dark between them. “My real name is Hana.”
The syllables settled into the quiet space, simple and un-sculpted by corporate patents.
“Jin-Young,” he answered, his thumb briefly pressing against the warm chrome seam of her wrist.
She pulled her hand back a fraction of a second before the main circuit caught. The soundstage flooded with blinding white light, washing the red shadows from the walls in a single pulse. When the Wuxing floor manager shoved the door open with a tablet in hand, Hana was already sitting upright with her posture straight and her chin lifted, eyes wide and smiling for the broadcast lens, while Tanaka Ryo stood by the door, his face slipping effortlessly back into immaculate corporate poise.

title: Sabotage
text:
The sub-floor dressing room beneath the Singapore mega-dome sat forty feet below the coastal water table, encased in six-foot slabs of vibration-dampened ferrocrete. Outside the climate envelope, the heavy equatorial heat of the Malacca Straits pressed against the reclaimed shoreline, but down in the prep trenches, the air was chilled to a dry, sterile eighteen degrees. Through the reinforced observation viewport overlooking the staging gantry, Tanaka Ryo watched two Mitsuhama corporate mages secure an inductive copper collar around Hana’s neck. The technicians worked in silence, their charcoal coats bearing the crimson triple-rhombus of Mitsuhama Media Logistics. Their sensor gloves glowed pale emerald as they calibrated the resonance couplings, tuning the frequencies until the secondary stage conduit hummed with a low, sub-audible vibration that rattled loose bolts in the deck plates.
Hana stood motionless on the prep riser under flickering mercury vapor tubes. Her porcelain dermal seams caught the harsh downlight, throwing sharp reflections across the bare concrete walls. Her chin stayed angled toward the overhead acoustic baffle, cervical actuators clicking at two-second intervals as internal micro-fans vented heat from her vocal processors. Across her collarbones, the corporate serial numbers were inlaid in microscopic silver foil: MCI-EXP-884-LUNA.
Beside Ryo’s vanity mirror, the stage logistics feed scrolled in amber characters across the glass: Unit 7 // Broadcast Apex // Full Resonance Extraction // Terminal Encore.
“Sixty seconds to lift locks,” the floor manager’s voice came through his earpiece, flat and clipped against the muffled seismic rumble overhead. “Ten-No-Koe choreography engages on the downbeat. Clear the gantry.”
Ryo stepped away from the glass. In the vanity mirror, Tanaka Ryo stared back: charcoal tunic tailored to the millimeter with silver silk piping, shoulders broadened by structural bio-sculpting, dark hair parted with razor-sharp corporate geometry. Beneath the immaculate exterior, his larynx carried the dull, grinding ache of the vocal shift, the cartilage held rigid against the instinct to soften into Lee Ji-yoo’s lighter cadence. He checked the magnetic seals on his stage cuffs. High above his left shoulder in the astral space, the bound watcher spirit hovered—a cold draft that tracked his core temperature, his blood pressure, and the cadence of his pulse, reporting every physiological deviation straight to the security node in Kyoto.
“Ten seconds,” the floor manager said.
Ryo walked out onto the central staging platform. The copper conductor plate under his boots was chilled from the subterranean cooling coils, etched with concentric geometric spirals that channeled directly into the primary geomantic lines running beneath the arena foundation. Ji-Hoon stood at the northern riser, his chrome forearm casings gleaming under the staging floods. Tae-Hyun adjusted his lacquered wolf mask at the eastern mark, while Min-Ki checked his footing on the western boundary plate. None of them spoke. Speech outside the designated broadcast telemetry carried automatic behavioral penalty deductions against their quarterly talent trusts.
The lift engaged with a heavy hydraulic hiss. The sub-floor acoustic drivers pumped seventy tons of sound pressure through the alloy platform, vibrating straight through his shins into his jaw. The lift breached the stage deck, rising through the floor into the blinding glare of the daylight arrays. Eighty-five thousand voices hit him like a physical wall. The crowd packed the tiered terraces beneath the smart-glass dome, a vast sea of synchronized glow-sticks and flashing AR banners undulating under the humid equatorial haze. Mitsuhama Media corporate holograms fifty feet high rotated in the stadium airspace, projecting the idol unit’s faces into the clouds.

Ji-Hoon hit the northern apex, limbs snapping into position as his internal cybernetics hummed in sync with the heavy synth-percussion. Tae-Hyun drove the eastern harmony, his wolf mask throwing sharp blue shadows across the first twenty rows, while Min-Ki anchored the western perimeter. Ryo crossed the center mark on count four, boots planting on the central conductor plate as the opening vocal line began.
The circuit closed. Eighty-five thousand minds surged into the channel. The sensation struck like a river of liquid fire. The geomantic siphon opened wide across the arena floor, harvesting the raw, uncritical adoration of eighty-five thousand spectators and funneling that emotional tidal wave straight through the stage risers. As the unit’s lead channel, Ryo became the biological lightning rod. The manufactured euphoria tore through his meridians with terrifying heat, expanding his aura until the spirit ribbons of his Musok training frayed under the sheer volume of collective desire. His voice rose into the arena’s quad-directional acoustic array, pure and effortless, riding the crest of the chorus while the telemetry monitors in his peripheral vision spiked deep into the red.
Through the white glare of the pyro flares, the secondary lift crested the stage floor. Hana rose on the sacrificial riser, framed in shimmering white brocade. The instant the staging conduit touched her copper collar, her cervical actuators locked with a sharp metallic snap. Her jaw was pulled upward, throat exposed to the daylight arrays as the Mitsuhama extraction protocol began tearing into her spiritual baseline. The crowd roared in response, mistaking her rigid, trembling posture and the radiant aura flare around her shoulders for an advanced holographic effect. The collective adoration of eighty-five thousand fans, channeled through Ryo’s voice, was being compressed and focused into her neck collar, stripping her essence to charge the corporate geomantic batteries buried in the arena foundation.
Ryo hit his turnaround at bar sixteen, spinning toward the center riser. Through the swirling stage smoke and strobes, he fixed on the porcelain seam along her cheek. Her breathing came in short, shallow gasps. Her eyes were wide, the optical shutters cycling erratically as the circuit burned through her neural firmware.
Then her gaze shifted, cutting through the sweep of automated broadcast drones, and locked directly onto his face.
The rehearsed stage-smile dropped from her lips. In the two seconds before the chorus peaked, her mouth formed a quiet, crooked curve—an un-scripted expression of recognition that answered his silence and released him from his marks.
Holding his position for eight more bars would allow the extraction to complete cleanly, leaving Hana an empty shell in the medical ward while Tanaka Ryo returned to his penthouse with his corporate contract intact. The logistics division would file the incident as an acute resonance burnout during a historic performance, paying out a modest survivor stipend to her registered relatives in Neo-Seoul.
At the crescendo, as eighty-five thousand voices crested in a synchronized roar, Ryo broke alignment. He dropped his chin, clamped his teeth until his jaw joints ground together, and wrenched the flow inward. He planted his heels hard against the copper plate, twisting his ankles to short-circuit the grounding trace, and routed eighty-five thousand channels of raw, un-buffered emotional energy straight into his own bone and adept channels, severing the feed to the stage capacitors.
The backlash struck like an iron slab through his skull. His spirit conduits surged against the flood, spirit ribbons violently untangling as the sheer volume of un-filtered mana overloaded his nervous system. The inductive copper plate beneath his boots superheated, the alloy warping with a screech of shearing rivets. The synthetic leather of his boots melted into smoldering resin against his soles. White sparks showered the front rows. Along the perimeter of the dome, the geomantic storage capacitors detonated in a sequence of deafening concussions, tearing structural pylons from their concrete footings and blowing fifty-foot sheets of flame into the access corridors.
The arena transformers screamed and blew. The Singapore mega-dome plunged into total, suffocating darkness. The music died mid-note, replaced by the sound of tearing speakers and eighty-five thousand voices collapsing from synthetic euphoria into blind, stampeding panic under the shattered ceiling.
Ryo hit the smoking stage deck. The electrical surge tore through his chest, locking his lungs in a violent spasm while the acrid stench of scorched insulation and vaporized circuit boards filled the air. Red emergency beacons flickered to life along the catwalks, painting the rising smoke in bloody streaks. Through the haze, corp-sec alarms began their rhythmic wail. Tactical mages in the wings shouted over dead radio channels, scrambling to contain the crowd as the smart-glass dome above began to crack under the acoustic shockwave.
He rolled off the shattered riser, landing hard in the debris-filled service trench beneath the stage platform. Blistered fingers dragged across jagged concrete until they hooked the iron ring of a drainage hatch. He hauled the iron cover back with a guttural heave and dropped into the dark.
He plunged into waist-deep brackish seawater and industrial runoff in the storm culvert beneath the arena foundation. The cold hit his scorched skin like a sheet of needles. In the pitch blackness of the sewer, Ryo ripped the smoking Mitsuhama tunic from his shoulders, tearing the embroidered silver piping and letting the oil-slicked water wash away the stage foundation and grey streaks of sweat from his neck. Above him, the rumble of the panicked stadium faded into the distant drone of harbor sirens.
The bound watcher spirit was gone, incinerated in the geomantic backlash. His commlink lay dead in the sludge. Wading against the tide of seawater, hands stinging from fresh electrical burns across his palms, Ryo pushed through the subterranean channels toward the container docks at Jurong—nameless, stripped of his corporate skin, and stepping into the shadows on his own terms.

title: First Negotiation
text:
Tanaka Ryo kept the unbadged Suzuki idling between his knees in the Redmond alley, the engine’s rhythmic vibration rattling loose fairing bolts against the cold steel frame. Across the polarized visor of his Shoei helmet, pirated AR spam flickered through the sulfur drizzle, with glitching advertisements for Stuffer Shack ramen and second-hand cyberware fighting for bandwidth in the local mesh. He cut the ignition with a turn of the key but left the helmet locked down tight over his chin. In the Barrens, bare features were an invitation to street violence; features sculpted with corporate symmetry were a magnetic disturbance that drew eyes from across a crowded room.
Inside the Red Line, sub-floor bass vibrated through the grease-stained floorboards from a jukebox looping thirty-year-old Neo-Tokyo synth-pop. Still wearing the dark, faceless dome of his riding helmet, he paused near a dead arcade terminal in the corner, shoulders slouched to mimic a delivery courier waiting on a delayed package. In the back booth beneath a flickering Shiawase promotional banner sat the Johnson, wearing a surplus wool overcoat with the frayed stitch scars of a NeoNet security patch cut from the lapel. The man nursed a glass of amber synthetic rye, his eyes darting between the front door and the bar taps with the ingrained nervousness of an ex-corporate middle manager stranded outside the grid.
Through the smoked shield of his visor, Ryo watched him in the scratched reflection of the arcade glass. When a heavy-set ork mercenary in armored ballistic plates pushed past the aisle, the Johnson’s aura flared with jagged, defensive orange, his right hand twitching toward an illegal pocket holster beneath his coat. But when the bar’s floor manager stepped over to clear an empty beer bottle, the man’s posture shifted instinctively—his spine straightened, chin dipping into the reflexive, ingrained deference of a salaryman accustomed to taking directives from executive suites. A masculine runner would trigger his panic and draw a defensive standoff; a corporate woman with clean, icy composure would slide beneath his guard and command the table.
Ryo slipped past the bar toward the narrow corridor leading to the rear storage rooms. The restroom was a damp concrete cell lit by a single buzzing fluorescent tube that threw grey shadows across stained tile. He locked the iron latch, unclipped the Shoei helmet, and set it on the water tank before stripping off his heavy riding leathers.
Then he initiated the shift.
His Transys Avalon commlink re-keyed the local PAN registers, broadcasting the clean, forged SIN of Lee Ji-yoo. The physical toll struck his marrow with dry, burning friction as the cosmetic spell engaged. Ryo gripped the cold porcelain edges of the sink, his knuckles whitening as the structural magic compressed his ribcage with a grinding ache. Height dropped from his spine, cartilage in his larynx settling with a heavy, audible click that thinned his breath to a lighter register. The bone-deep throb behind his eyes peaked as the jawline and cheekbones softened, settling into the smooth, delicate frame of Lee Ji-yoo.
She opened her eyes in the stained mirror, waiting for the momentary vertigo to clear. She smoothed the dark silk shell over her narrowed shoulders, leaving the heavy riding jacket folded behind the exposed water pipes. She stepped into flat leather shoes, unlocked the door, and walked back out into the smoky gloom of the bar.
She slipped into the booth opposite the Johnson with silent, fluid grace.
The man looked up, his hand freezing on the rim of his glass as the red neon from the bar sign caught her face—clean, balanced, without a single blemish, scar, or line of street fatigue. His throat moved as he swallowed, his fingers slipping off the synthetic rye.
“You’re late,” he said, but the words carried no weight against the stillness across the table.
“Knight Errant sweeps were active along the perimeter highway,” Ji-yoo said, her voice clear, level, and entirely devoid of street slang. “The transit took longer to avoid automated checkpoints.”
The Johnson cleared his throat and slid a battered Sony datapad across the cedar laminate. “Renraku storage node in Bellevue. Ten thousand nuyen. Five thousand up front for operational expenses, five on delivery.”
Ji-yoo glanced at the encrypted node coordinates on the screen, then rested her hands flat and open on the table. “Eight thousand,” she said.
The Johnson blinked, his brow furrowing as he leaned back. “What?”
“Eight thousand,” she repeated, her tone calm and conversational. “And no advance.”
The Johnson pulled back into the corner of the booth, his eyes narrowing with sharp corporate suspicion. Street runners fought over every scrip, demanding up-front deposits for ammo, forged credentials, and decker fees. A runner who negotiated the price downward was an operative with an unstated agenda.
“Runners don’t negotiate down,” the Johnson said, his grip tightening on the table edge. “Who are you working for?”
“Clean retrieval,” Ji-yoo said, holding his gaze with unblinking composure. “Renraku will not log the intrusion as an external breach. When the datapad is delivered, you owe me a marker. One favor, on demand, within your departmental authority.”
The Johnson sat motionless. The immediate relief of saving corporate operating budget died, replaced by the heavy understanding of personal debt. Nuyen was spent and forgotten; a personal marker stayed on the books forever. He looked at the quiet poise across the table, the complete absence of street desperation, and gave a single, tight nod.
“One marker,” he said, sliding the pad fully across the wood. “We have an agreement.”
Ji-yoo picked up the datapad, slipped it into her coat pocket, and stood. She walked out into the Redmond drizzle, leaving the Johnson alone with his synthetic rye beneath the glitching neon.

title: Seattle Web
text:
From the flat gravel roof of the four-story Redmond tenement, the Wuxing needle cut a slender emerald mark against the low sulfur cloud cover over downtown Seattle. Cold rain drummed steadily against the rusted corrugated housing of an industrial roof exhaust, pooling in grease-stained puddles around Ryo’s boots. He sat on the iron casing with his Transys Avalon commlink resting between his knees, its diagnostic display casting pale blue light across his wet leather riding trousers. Thirty feet below in the alleyway, the muffled hum of a pirated power transformer vibrated through the brickwork, competing with the distant wail of a Knight Errant patrol siren on the perimeter highway.
To lock the encrypted transmission against local grid sweeps, he released the active Cosmetic Control spell, letting the shaping magic drain from his facial tissue. Ribs widened with a deep, grinding ache as his chest expanded to its native volume, the compressed bone settling into its true frame. Cartilage along his jawline broadened with a heavy, wet click, the artificial symmetry of Tanaka Ryo dissolving as solid obsidian color pooled back into the outer rims of his irises. For the first time in three weeks, he breathed through the raw, un-sculpted lungs of Kim Jin-Young.
He initiated the encrypted hand-shake protocol. The signal jumped through three separate dead-letter relays across Denver, Vladivostok, and Hong Kong before locking onto an optical node in the Neo-Seoul network. The Avalon’s holo-emitter whirred, projecting a high-resolution terminal feed into the rainy dark.
The display stabilized.
Hana sat in an opulent, high-floor executive suite within the Wuxing Seoul Arcology, framed by floor-to-ceiling smart-glass looking out over the glowing neon sea of the Gangnam district. She wore a tailored white silk blazer over an emerald blouse, her dark hair swept up and secured with polished jade pins. Dermal plating along her collarbones gleamed beneath warm golden architectural lighting, the silver serial numbers polished until they caught the light like fine jewelry. Her cervical actuators were completely silent, upgraded to executive-grade hydraulic silent-runners that produced no mechanical tick.
“Jin-Young,” she said, her voice rich, resonant, and entirely stripped of the breathy fragility he remembered from the soundstages. Her optical shutters cycled once, tracking the low-light feed from the Redmond roof.
“The routing is clean,” he said, speaking in his unmasked baseline voice. “The courier in Tacoma cleared the credstick drop yesterday. Twelve thousand nuyen in certified scrip. It should cover the medical retainer for your cervical servos through the winter.”
Hana looked directly into the camera array, her expression composed with the serene, untouchable authority of a corporate vice-president reviewing quarterly performance charts. “You shouldn’t have called,” she said quietly. “And you shouldn’t have sent the money.”
Ryo’s fingers tightened on the alloy edge of the commlink casing, rain dripping from his chin onto the glass. “The courier had clean credentials. What happened?”
“Wuxing didn’t intercept the drop, Jin,” she said, her voice smooth and devoid of panic. “They cleared the payment through their primary banking node. Your entire courier chain in Seattle operates on their talent retention budget.”
The rain seemed to grow heavier around him, washing over the gravel in cold, grey sheets.
“Mitsuhama and Wuxing signed a joint security accord three months ago,” she continued, her gaze steady across the trans-Pacific link. “They aren’t hunting you through the Barrens with tactical kill-teams. They promoted me to senior creative director for Pan-Asian Media. My face is projected across fifty-story holograms in every sector from Neo-Tokyo to Singapore. They gave me this suite, these upgrades, and this title because their actuarial models calculated that your emerging empathy would keep you looking back.”
A cold, hollow weight opened in the center of his chest.
“Every payment you sent through Tacoma, every encrypted relay you bought from Seattle deckers, and every shadow contract you completed was logged on a Wuxing server,” she said. “They used your concern as the exact breadcrumb trail to map your entire network in the sprawl. They know your safehouses, your contacts, and your street docs. The contracts to reclaim both of us under joint corporate ownership are already drafted and sitting on the board table.”
Ryo sat motionless in the dark, the rain soaking through his collar, freezing against the bare skin of his neck. The quiet sanctuaries he thought he had been building—the noodles with Pavel, the tea in Tacoma with Ni Ni Xiaolu, the quiet payments sent across the Pacific—had not bought safety or distance. They had been converted into corporate telemetry, turning his first fragile attempts at human compassion into the very cage designed to drag him back.
“They’re waiting for you to exhaust yourself,” Hana said, her voice softening by a fraction of a degree. “When you realize you can’t run far enough, they expect you to walk into the Seattle consulate and sign the joint agreement.”
“Hana,” he began, but the words caught in his dry throat.
“My name is Director Yueying now,” she said, the polite, unbreakable corporate smile returning to her porcelain lips. “Do not transmit to this node again.”
Ryo sat in the dark as the sulfur wind came off the Barrens, listening to the rain beat against the rusted sheet metal eaves. In the distance, the emerald needle of the Wuxing tower pulsed through the low clouds, cold and untouchable above the sprawl.
He stood up, wet gravel grinding beneath his boots.
He dropped the Avalon commlink onto the concrete, raised his heel, and drove the heavy riding sole down into the glass until the alloy buckled and the processors shorted in a brief shower of orange sparks. He kicked the scrap into the rain gutter, pulled his collar high against the damp wind, and took the fire escape down into the dark.

title: Bliss
text:
Beneath the West Seattle elevated freight overpass, automated cargo haulers rumbled across steel expansion joints every sixty seconds, sending a deep shudder through the rusted framework of the roadside noodle cart. Cold rain dripped from the torn vinyl awning into the curb drain, hissing against the cast-iron burner where forty gallons of rich pork-bone broth simmered in a heavy aluminum cauldron. Velvet sat on the corner wooden stool, wrapped in a dark oilskin slicker, wearing the street persona of Mei Jing. Faded blue syndicate ink traced the tendons of her right wrist and rose along the left side of her jaw beneath the upturned canvas collar.
On the cedar counter next to her steaming bowl sat the credstick basket from the Octagon Triad courier. Resting in the corner of the weave was a single unopened Bliss capsule wrapped in silver yin-yang foil, fifteen nuyen of synthetic chemical numbness meant as a gratuity for the courier’s run. She picked up the small cylinder, turning the plastic between her bare fingers before setting it back beside the broth. Across the counter, the elderly cook lowered fresh wheat noodles into boiling water with a wire basket, the rising steam creating a warm, clouded pocket of air that held the rain at bay.
Water splashed in the gutter as heavy boots dragged along the pavement. A man stumbled into the shelter of the awning, wearing a waterlogged canvas work jacket where the Russian Vory insignia on the left shoulder had been violently hacked off with a combat blade, leaving frayed grey threads hanging over torn ballistic weave. He slumped onto the stool two seats away, his raw, bruised hands trembling against the wooden counter as he fought to steady his breathing.
“Broth,” the man rasped, his vocal cords raw from the aftereffects of inhaled aerosol sedatives. “Hot.”
The cook slid a heavy ceramic bowl across the cedar wood without asking for creds up front. The man reached for a pair of bamboo chopsticks from the stoneware jar, but his twitching fingers lost their grip, sending the sticks clattering across the wet laminate. He stared down at his swollen knuckles, his forearms still suffering involuntary tremors from the electrical nerve-blocker Velvet had driven into his cervical cluster thirty-six hours earlier during the geothermal plant breach in Puyallup.
He turned his head slowly, bloodshot eyes fixing on the woman sitting two stools away.
His breath hitched in his throat as he recognized the faded ink along her jawline and the unnerving, motionless calm in her dark eyes. His right hand jerked instinctively toward an empty armpit holster before remembering that his heavy Ceska submachine gun was currently buried beneath ten feet of toxic sludge in the flooded plant sump. The man was Pavel, the young Vory combat mage who had broken under fire as the perimeter wards collapsed around the illicit narcotics lab.
“You,” Pavel whispered, his voice trembling as he pressed his back hard against the cart’s support pole.
Velvet did not reach for a weapon, nor did her posture tighten into a combat stance. She held his gaze across the steaming counter with quiet, level stillness, her hands resting open beside her ceramic bowl.
“Drink the broth,” she said, her voice low, steady, and carrying the soothing cadence of Lee Ji-yoo. “The chili oil clears the chemical residue from the lungs.”
Pavel swallowed hard, his chest heaving under the damp canvas jacket as he looked between her open hands and the steaming soup. “I know the containment formulas,” he blurted out, the words spilling past his lips in a rush of shame and exhausted panic. “I bound a hearth-spirit when I was fourteen in Vladivostok. I had the chalk circle drawn on the concrete. But the mana tore away the second I spoke the binding mantra. The spirit wouldn’t take form.”
He wiped his mouth with a soaked sleeve, his eyes bright with the terror of a syndicate soldier awaiting execution. “I froze. Before your strike team breached the iron doors, my magic was already dead in my hands. If the Vory elders think I choked on a basic third-circle summon, they’ll weigh my boots with scrap iron and dump me in the Duwamish river before sunrise.”
Velvet looked at the young mage, his skin grey and hollow under the single yellow work bulb hanging from the cart awning.
She picked up her bowl, letting the ceramic heat soak into her palms. “The geothermal plant was built directly over the Puyallup ash beds,” Velvet said quietly. “Surrounded by subterranean coal fires, heavy industrial slag, and un-filtered chemical runoff from the old refineries. The ground water beneath the floor was saturated with industrial mercury. The local background count was screaming pollution at a level four severity.”
Pavel blinked, his trembling hands freezing over the wooden counter as the technical explanation registered.
“Your chalk circle was structurally intact,” Velvet continued, her tone matter-of-fact and calm. “Your vocal gesture was clean. The mana broke because the earth beneath your boots was poisoned. No mage in Seattle summons a clean hearth-spirit out of industrial sewage without suffering severe drain backlash.”
Pavel sat completely motionless on the stool. His shoulders slowly sank, the white-knuckled grip on his knees relaxing as he let out a long, ragged breath that mixed with the rising steam.
“You took a stray sedative dart during the initial breach,” Velvet added, her dark eyes meeting his with steady assurance. “You were knocked unconscious while holding the northern access corridor. Tell your brigadier that story, and keep your head down until the heat clears.”
Pavel looked down at his hands, finding them steady for the first time in two days. He picked up a fresh pair of chopsticks from the jar, dipped them into the dark broth, and pulled noodles to his mouth.
They sat together beneath the rattling awning as the rain poured over the West Seattle overpass, eating hot noodles in the quiet shelter away from the sprawl, leaving the silver Bliss capsule untouched in the credstick basket.

title: Tea in Tacoma
text:
Salt fog off Commencement Bay rolled up the dark slope of the Tacoma waterfront, wrapping around the low wooden eaves of Xingfu Chaguan and muffling the rhythmic clang of container cranes out in the deep-water harbor. Inside the private rear tea room, the mechanical roar of the industrial sprawl fell away, replaced by the gentle hiss of water reaching a simmer in a cast-iron kettle over a bed of glowing hardwood charcoal. Old-growth cedar panels lined the walls, insulated with acoustic damping and copper mesh that blocked external Matrix feeds, wireless transceivers, and optical surveillance drones. The air carried the dry, earthy fragrance of roasted oolong and warm cedar resin.
Tanaka Ryo sat on a low tatami cushion across from Ni Ni Xiaolu, his posture held in his masculine baseline profile with his shoulders square under an unbadged charcoal silk overcoat. Across the low cedar table, Ni Ni Xiaolu sat with immaculate poise in a tailored black blazer over ivory silk, her dark hair swept up and fastened with antique bone pins. She watched him over the rim of a small celadon cup, the stillness in her frame carrying the hard-won vigilance of an Octagon Triad Red Pole who had survived three separate syndicate purges along the Seattle waterfront.
Between them on the cedar wood, resting precisely six inches from her right hand, lay her customized Ares Predator heavy pistol, its mother-of-pearl grip catching the amber glow of the charcoal burner. Outside the rice-paper sliding door, the heavy silhouette of Teddy Chin stood post in the corridor, his cybernetic arms crossed over his chest.
Ni Ni set the clay teapot down with a soft, deliberate click against the cedar tray. “The Cutters have pulled their enforcers back from the West Seattle bridge,” she said, her voice smooth, level, and quiet in the enclosed space. “Bookie’s Ancients agreed to keep their bike patrols east of the river. And Baxter’s bootleg Bliss refinery in Puyallup is cold slag.”
She paused, her dark eyes fixing on the calm symmetry of his face with sharp, analytical appraisal.
“My courier brought back the credstick basket from the noodle cart,” she continued, her tone conversational yet probing. “You left the Bliss capsule on the street.”
“Counterfeits poison the market, Ms. Xiaolu,” Ryo said, his voice resonant and steady. “Yours and mine. An asset who relies on synthetic numbness makes mistakes on the operational perimeter.”
Ni Ni studied him across the rising steam, tracking the steady line of his jaw, the complete absence of nervous micro-tremors, and the quiet focus in his dark eyes. “Who engineered you, Mr. Tanaka?” she asked softly. “Was it Mitsuhama? Or did Wuxing send a bio-sculpted asset to listen through my cedar walls?”
Her right hand slid across the polished cedar table, her manicured fingers coming to rest lightly over the pearl grip of the heavy Predator.
Ryo did not reach for an internal holster, nor did the muscles in his neck tighten into a defensive posture. He deliberately allowed his active presence to settle into neutral stillness, releasing the subtle spell-tension behind his jaw so that his aura radiated calm, un-engineered composure. He reached out with bare, steady hands, lifted his celadon cup, and took a slow sip of the dark, steaming tea.
“No corporation sent me to you, Ms. Xiaolu,” Ryo said, setting the cup back onto the cedar tray without making a sound. He met her gaze across the table, his hands resting open and flat on the wood. “I operate in the Seattle shadows because I refuse to take directives from corporate boardrooms.”
Silence settled across the cedar-lined room, filled only by the quiet bubbling of the iron kettle and the distant, mournful groan of a foghorn out in the bay. Ni Ni’s fingers remained on the pearl weapon grip for three slow, measured breaths. Then her hand withdrew, settling flat in her lap beneath the edge of the table.
Her shoulders sank slightly, the rigid tension along her collarbone easing as she lifted her teapot with both hands, pouring a fresh stream of amber liquid into his cup.
“The leaves are harvested from old bushes near Ningbo,” she murmured, watching the steam rise against the wood ceiling. “Smuggled across the Pacific in dry cargo containers without corporate tariffs.”
“It tastes of clean iron and rain,” Ryo said, nodding in quiet appreciation.
They sat together in the warm, cedar-lined room as the Puget Sound drizzle drummed softly against the roof tiles, drinking un-monetized tea in the quiet space away from the sprawl. When Ryo stood to depart, he left two certified credsticks on the edge of the table for the tea master, bowed with respectful corporate economy, and stepped out into the cold Tacoma salt fog.

title: Story Arc 1: The Anatomy of Un-Manufactured Solace & The Honeytrap
text:
Master Theme: The Anatomy of Un-Manufactured Solace
To capture the gentle, melancholic warmth of Best Wishes from the Full Moon Coffee Shop within the violent, commodified dystopia of Shadowrun, the overarching narrative needs a unifying thematic spine—a quiet, emotional current running beneath the rain, gunplay, and corporate intrigue.
In the Sixth World, where every emotion, face, and sensation is engineered, packaged, and sold, authentic comfort is the rarest luxury in existence.
Velvet’s unique perspective provides the ideal infrastructure for this contrast: engineered by Mitsuhama to be a Charisma 12 miracle of mass-market desire, Velvet understands the exact chemistry and fraud behind synthetic happiness.
Instead of treating Charisma 12 as a corporate tractor beam or an offensive weapon, Velvet slowly learns to invert their training. In the quiet aftermath of dark shadowruns, Velvet creates brief, un-engineered moments where the desperate people of the Sprawl—gangers, corporate Johnsons, street docs, and allies—can lay down their masks without fear of being exploited.
This master theme unfolds across three interconnected narrative threads:

title: Story Arc 1: The Anatomy of Un-Manufactured Solace & The Honeytrap
text:
Core Concept: In a world where everything warm is a subscription model or an addiction, a runaway corporate asset uses their unearthly, manufactured presence not to extract or control, but to create fleeting, un-monetized sanctuaries for broken people—discovering his own capacity for empathy in the process, before the brutal reality of the corporate trap closes in.





Thread 1: The Currency of “Real Bliss” (The Counter-Product)

Thematic Grounding: In Bootleg Bliss, Dwight Baxter tried to sell cheap, counterfeit drugs using a Triad’s name to make people feel safe. Mitsuhama sells bio-sculpted idols; Wuxing sells mass-market spiritual highs; BTL pushers sell digital dreams. Everyone in Seattle is hooked on a different form of “Bootleg Bliss” to survive the Barrens.
The Character Arc: Having been built as a product meant to induce parasocial devotion, Velvet realizes that true solace cannot be mass-produced. Over the course of the campaign, Velvet’s side interactions are defined by offering small, authentic sensory anchors—a bowl of hand-pulled noodle broth on a cold night, a quiet cup of un-synthesized tea, or simply sitting in silence without deploying an aura-siphon.
The Moving Realization: Velvet begins to collect these small, un-engineered moments like hidden treasures. In a city where everything is logged and monetized, a quiet, un-recorded conversation over real food becomes the ultimate act of shadow-rebellion and the cradle of his emerging empathy.




Thread 2: The Sanctuary of the Un-Sculpted Space

Thematic Grounding: Velvet’s physical existence is a constant, agonizing biological shift between Lee Ji-yoo and Tanaka Ryo, with bone cartilage resetting and localized DNA strands re-keying. The corporate machine insists that Jin-Young no longer exists.
The Existential Horror of the Engineered Aura: When someone is in the room with an engineered asset whose voice, bone symmetry, and aura are designed to warp emotions, it is impossible for them to know whether their feelings (pity, trust, attraction) are genuine or the product of an invisible biological manipulation. Hardened street contacts feel an instinctive, suffocating paranoia around Velvet because they cannot trust their own minds.
The Character Arc & Sanctuary: The quiet, bruised space between transformations—when active spells fade, Charisma is deliberately suppressed, and the true, un-sculpted self breathes—is where genuine connection becomes possible. By consciously refusing to manipulate people and stepping down from the engineered gravity, Velvet creates rare sanctuaries where figures like Ni Ni Xiaolu, Pavel, or Whiskey can finally drop their defenses without fear of being exploited. In doing so, Velvet slowly discovers his own missing humanity.




Thread 3: The Gilded Honeytrap & The Dual-Megacorp Trap (The Climax)

Thematic Grounding: Hana (“Luna”) lives in Neo-Seoul in a gilded, Wuxing-executive penthouse suite, her face projected across Asian media nodes. Velvet believes she is a captive whose safety he is covertly funding and nurturing through encrypted channels and quiet sensory anchors.
The Dramatic Irony & The Trap: Unknown to Velvet during his early Seattle runs, Hana’s comfortable imprisonment is not an accident—she is the curated bait in a joint, high-stakes corporate play between Mitsuhama and Wuxing. Mitsuhama wants their runaway multi-million nuyen asset back; Wuxing wants to harvest Velvet’s unique engineered geomantic mana conduit. Both megacorps calculated that Velvet’s emerging emotional attachment to Hana would keep him predictable, using his secret payments, shadow runs, and communications as the exact breadcrumb trail to trace his network.
The Climax Reveal: Story Arc 1 climaxes with the devastating revelation that Hana’s gilded cage was constructed from the beginning as a dual-megacorp honeytrap. The discovery shatters Velvet’s illusion that he could quietly buy her freedom or live in low-profile evasion, forcing a complete pivot into the Seattle underground for Arc 2.

title: Story Arc 2: The Sovereign Underground & The Push for Power
text:
Master Theme: Sovereign Leverage in the Deep Sprawl
Following the devastating revelation at the climax of Story Arc 1—that Hana’s gilded penthouse in Neo-Seoul was weaponized as a joint honeytrap by Mitsuhama and Wuxing—Velvet abandons the naive illusion of low-profile evasion.
Story Arc 2 chronicles Velvet’s emergence into the deep Seattle underground and his relentless, strategic drive to amass enough magical, financial, and political power to survive against two predatory megacorps playing decadal chess.
In Arc 1, Velvet learned what empathy was by building un-monetized sanctuaries. In Arc 2, Velvet learns that sanctuaries must be defended with teeth. He transitions from a fleeing corporate fugitive into an authoritative, formidable shadow operator—an Adept Face who commands respect across syndicate backrooms, smuggling routes, and magical conclaves.

title: Story Arc 2: The Sovereign Underground & The Push for Power
text:
Key Narrative Pillars & Campaign Threads

Thread 1: The Descent into the Unmapped Sub-Sprawl

Thematic Grounding: Surface Seattle is monitored by corporate grids, facial-recognition drone fleets, and orbital tracking. To slip the dual-megacorp dragnet, Velvet relocates core operations into the subterranean depths—the Ork Underground, abandoned pre-Crash transit tunnels, and Seattle’s deep geothermal underbelly.
The Atmosphere: The slick, rain-drenched surface gives way to damp basalt caverns, glowing sulfur pipes, illicit black-market bazaars, and hidden shamanic shrines. Here, corporate jurisdiction is zero and personal reputation is the only currency that matters.
The Transformation: Velvet constructs true, fortified sanctuaries in the deep dark—places where outcasts, runners, and allies find genuine protection under his growing influence.




Thread 2: The Relentless Push for Power (Magical & Financial Accumulation)

Thematic Grounding: Charisma 12 and weaponized charm are formidable, but corporate strike teams pack high-threat bio-magic, null-zones, and heavy armor. Velvet needs overwhelming personal and magical force.
Magical Evolution: Velvet accelerates his Shinto-Musok initiation path:

Mastering Channeling to house ancestral spirits directly within his physical frame.
Embracing Invocation to summon and bind formidable Great Form spirits, deepening ritual authority and esoteric deterrence.
Unlocking deeper spiritual resonance to anchor local leylines without corporate ritual hardware.

Financial & Gear Scaling: Pushing for veteran and prime-tier shadowruns to build massive capital reserves, acquiring military-grade commlinks, qi foci, and specialized talismans.




Thread 3: Syndicate Pacts & Mutual Deterrence

Thematic Grounding: No runner survives two megacorps alone. Velvet leverages his diplomatic genius and unearthly presence to broker interlocking alliances across Seattle’s criminal factions:

The Octagon Triad (Ni Ni Xiaolu): Deepening a mutual partnership founded on authentic respect, trading high-level corporate intelligence for Triad muscle and smuggling corridors.
The Cutters (Trudy): Empowering street-level gang networks to serve as early-warning sensor arrays across Redmond and Puyallup.
The Ancients (Bookie): Securing high-speed courier lines and elven underworld solidarity across the Tacoma docks.
The Guild of Freelance Assets / Shinto-Musok Conclave: Solidifying coven standing and ancestral backing.

The Strategic Realization: By weaving himself into the economic and magical fabric of Seattle’s underworld, attacking Velvet ceases to be a simple asset recovery; it threatens an all-out underworld war that neither Mitsuhama nor Wuxing can afford to ignite.




Thread 4: Redefining the Counter-Strike (The Long Game for Hana)

Thematic Grounding: Hana is no longer an innocent victim to be bought out with credsticks; she is a high-profile corporate prisoner at the center of a geopolitical web.
The Character Arc: Velvet stops sending naive messages that corporate spiders can trace. Instead, he begins building an asymmetric, multi-vector strike network—identifying Wuxing and Mitsuhama rivalries, planting sleeper assets in Neo-Seoul, and preparing the groundwork for a decadal strike that will sever Hana’s corporate bonds once and for all.
